repo.description:
SurrealDB record access methods defined `WITH REFRESH` issue a refresh token that a client can later exchange for new access tokens. The `revoke` RPC method invalidates such a refresh token. That method performed no authentication and no proof of possession: it took the target namespace, database, and access method from an access token that was decoded without verifying its signature, took the grant identifier from a refresh string that was only format-checked, and then carried out the revocation as root. It never verified that the caller actually held the refresh token's key.

A grant identifier is not a secret. `ACCESS <ac> SHOW ALL` reveals every grant's `id` (only the key is redacted) and requires only `VIEWER`-level view permission on the access method, and the identifier is embedded in every issued refresh token. So any caller who learned a grant identifier - a low-privileged database user, or anyone to whom a token leaked - could permanently revoke the corresponding refresh token without holding its key. This turned an operation that over SurrealQL (`ACCESS ... REVOKE GRANT`) requires the Owner role into one reachable by a low-privileged, or in principle unauthenticated, RPC caller.

The victim's refresh token was then permanently invalidated: every subsequent refresh failed, forcing re-authentication.

### Impact

This affects deployments that use record access methods defined `WITH REFRESH` and expose the `/rpc` endpoint (the default), where an attacker can learn a grant identifier - for example through any database-level account (including `VIEWER`) via `ACCESS <ac> SHOW ALL`, or through a leaked refresh token.

What an attacker **can** do:

- Permanently revoke another user's refresh token by supplying its grant identifier to the `revoke` RPC, without holding the token's key.
- Enumerate all grant identifiers for an access method with only `VIEWER`-level view permission, and revoke every user's refresh token for that method, denying refresh to all of its users.

What it **can't** do:

- Recover the refresh token's key, sign in as the victim, or read the victim's data - this is not account takeover or data disclosure. The victim can re-authenticate with their credentials.
- Guess a grant identifier without a disclosure channel; the identifier carries roughly 68 bits of entropy, so a low-privilege or token-leak channel is required in practice.
- Affect deployments that do not use `WITH REFRESH`.

### Patches

Revoking a refresh token now requires proof of possession. The presented refresh key is verified with a constant-time comparison against the stored grant - the same check the refresh (sign-in) path already performs - before anything is revoked, so only the holder of the token (or an Owner acting through SurrealQL) can revoke it. Every failure is reported as an opaque authentication error, so a caller cannot distinguish a wrong key from a missing, expired, or already-revoked grant.

- Versions 3.3.0 and later are not affected by this issue.

### Workarounds

Users unable to patch should consider the following workarounds:

- Deny the `revoke` RPC method via capabilities where refresh-token revocation is not required (for example `--deny-rpc revoke`, env `SURREAL_CAPS_DENY_RPC`).
- Restrict network access to the `/rpc` endpoint to trusted clients.
- Treat grant identifiers as sensitive: limit who holds database-level accounts that can run `ACCESS <ac> SHOW ALL`, since it discloses grant identifiers.

### References

- [SurrealQL Documentation - DEFINE ACCESS](https://surrealdb.com/docs/surrealql/statements/define/access)
- [SurrealDB Documentation - RPC protocol](https://surrealdb.com/docs/surrealdb/integration/rpc)
- [SurrealDB Documentation - Capabilities](https://surrealdb.com/docs/surrealdb/security/capabilities)
- `fix(iam): require proof of possession to revoke a refresh token` (included in SurrealDB 3.3.0)

### Acknowledgements

Thank you to [Yanhaoxi](https://github.com/Yanhaoxi) for reporting this issue.
repo.summary: The `revoke` RPC invalidates any user's refresh token without authentication or proof of possession
